title: The fellowship of the grind
summary: 'It was moving to watch, and a little shaming that, in this industry and in this country, working musicians can depend only on each other'

blocks.text: In my first week of college in Manila, I went looking for the nearest, and cheapest, folk house in the University Belt. It was 1978 and the scene was in full bloom. Once my campus paper allowance kicked in, I graduated from the folk houses of Recto and Morayta to Ermita, the mecca, the venues we read about in Jingle Magazine: Kola House, Hobbit House, My Father’s Mustache.

Beer was cold and nobody minded the smoke. The sets ran from the ’60s canon of Bob Dylan, Peter, Paul and Mary, and Simon & Garfunkel, the gritty folk of Neil Young, the two-part harmonies of Seals & Crofts and Loggins & Messina, to the acoustic pop of James Taylor and Jim Croce, the bruised love songs of Jackson Browne, and the country-folk of John Denver.

But the folk house was never just about the music, particularly after the declaration of martial law in 1972. These intimate venues, usually a dim room with one singer and perhaps thirty listeners, became one of the few places where young people could gather, listen to “Blowin’ In The Wind” or “He Was My Brother” and other socially relevant songs, and not look over their shoulders. They provided sanctuary for the weary, the worried, and the dreamers.
Behind the performances was a grind.

Pendong Aban Jr. of Asin got his first gig at Charcoal House on Recto in the early ‘70s with his friend Keith. As Keith and Fred, they played two sets a night for P20 each. Charcoal House, however, was pang-masa, a student hangout; someone told them they were ready for Mabini, where the serious folk houses were.
At their audition at Pension Filipina, they watched God’s Ego, the heavy hitters known for spot-on Crosby, Stills and Nash covers. They realized they were not ready for Mabini yet.

By 1975, Keith and Fred were regulars at Kola House, My Father’s Mustache, Bodega, and Pension Filipina. Aban eventually went solo and did gigs in Japan. Back from a six-month stint, Aban alternated sets with a trio composed of Mike Pillora, Cesar Bañares, and a Manila-born singer with a big, soulful voice, Lolita Carbon. The three were Salt of the Earth, packing rooms with Peter, Paul and Mary covers. Aban’s solo set was eclectic, with covers of David Bowie’s “Space Oddity” and Dylan’s “Masters of War” and “Hurricane.”

Pillora, recalls Aban, invited him to play bass for the group, and that was the beginning of Asin. When “Anak” made Freddie Aguilar, another folk singer, a star, the labels came scouting the folk houses for the next big act, and one of them found the quartet.
A generation of Filipino musicians was made through gigs abroad, bands formed between sets, and countless auditions where competition was tight but friendly.

Chickoy Pura recalled those years at a recent benefit show his contemporaries staged for him at My Brother’s Mustache in Quezon City, perhaps the only remaining venue for folk songs and folk singers today. Folk singers of his time, said Pura, shared experiences, a bond, and sometimes guitars.

“Ang unang tanong sa iyo noong araw, ilan na ba ang pondo mo?” he recalled. A singer’s pondo was his stock of songs. Pura had maybe 15. Come back when you have 30, he was told. His first pay was a sandwich; later, P30 a night.
Today, he said, young players walk into bars with top-of-the-line gear. “Before, we looked for jobs on borrowed guitar sometimes.”
“We’re older now and some of our friends fell by the wayside, but we remember them with much affection and pride… You stop playing, you stop living,” he told the audience.

By the early ’80s, the mass market had drifted back to formula pop; the restless young channelled their restlessness through punk and heavy metal. Still, every eatery, canteen, or food court needed live entertainment, and folk singers came cheapest, although the songs have changed. I once sat through a lunchtime acoustic rendition of “Careless Whisper” in a busy student canteen.

The pioneers, their best years behind them, continue to make their living from shows that are few and far between. Those who landed record deals and delivered hit songs received meager royalties, if they came at all. The road takes its toll on voices and bodies, and many of them are well past retirement age. The medical bills begin to pile up.
What has never left is the fellowship. When one of them falls ill, the others play a benefit, as they always have, before small crowds of loyal, graying fans.

They were there that night for Pura. Lolita Carbon’s voice was powerful as ever, her stage presence still electric. It was also her birthday. The secret of life? “Basta masaya lang lagi dapat,” she told me after her set.

Lito Crisostomo, former lead guitarist for The Blank, Ang Grupong Pendong, and Asin, played Crosby, Stills and Nash classics with Erwin, his partner from their days in the circuit as Fat and Thin. For more than five hours, act after act took the stage: Bobby Mondejar and Friends, Corky and Kiko, Rene Vega, Albert de Pano, Koko Marbella, Pete Velasquez, Ding Laag, and Joel Yu. Special guests were Pido Lalimarmo, founding member of Side A and Artstart who now fronts an all-Steely Dan covers band Black Cows, as well as the Kakoy Legaspi Blues Collective, whose smoldering blues set prompted advertising maverick Vince Pozon to declare “may pag-asa pa sa kabataan.”

An extended jam on James Taylor’s “Steamroller Blues” rounded off the night of music and fellowship. By that time, it was almost 1 am but no one was in a hurry to leave. It was moving to watch, and a little shaming that, in this industry and in this country, working musicians can depend only on each other. The voice, the energy, the spirit, those things the grind could not take from them. – Rappler.com
